newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria poll seals consensus on reform - president.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria poll seals consensus on reform - president.

text.p: Bulgarian President Petar Stoyanov said on Thursday that parliamentary elections on Saturday will seal a new national consensus in favour of market reforms delayed since the end of communist rule.

Stoyanov, whose election last November marked the start of a process that culminated in mass demonstrations which ousted the Socialist government in February, predicted a stable reformist majority in the new parliament.

"The main achievement of this country over the past few months is not the peaceful solution to the crisis back in January but the fact that all political forces could be brought to sit around the same table and reach an agreement on these priorities," he told Reuters in an interview.

Saturday's elections are expected to bring to power the former opposition Union of Democratic Forces whose protest campaign toppled the ex-communist Socialists in February. The main question is how large a majority the UDF will get.
Stoyanov, 44, said Bulgaria was a latecomer to market reforms, but could learn from the mistakes of its more advanced ex-communist neighbours.

"Bulgarians learned their lessons from these seven years, first that they must put their house in order and tidy up their back yard before looking outside for help," said Stoyanov, who was elected on a pledge to bring Bulgaria closer to the European Union and NATO.
"They learned to believe in themselves, in their own potential and strength, and then turn for help, understanding and solidarity to Europe and the rest of the world."
After 30 days of mass protests fuelled by economic hardship, Stoyanov brokered an agreement in February between the main political parties for early elections.

The Socialists agreed to give up attempts to form a new government, and Stoyanov appointed an interim cabinet which negotiated a new accord with the International Monetary Fund, began the process of overhauling the economy, and cracked down on corruption and organised crime.
Under the terms of the IMF accord, the new government must introduce a currency board, a restrictive fixed exchange rate regime to restore monetary stability.
Privatisation and restructuring or closure of loss-making state enterprises has also been stepped up.
The popular president who took office in January has attracted a string of Western ministers, bankers and economists to Sofia to offer support and advice.
"There is a very genuine sentiment in favour of reform in this country at the moment," Stoyanov said.
He said the makeup of the new parliament was less important than how they approached the tasks ahead.
"They will have to shoulder all the responsibility for the difficult transition, face the reforms, immediately start conducting them and carry them on after the elections," he said.
